value.overview: The Common Pauraque is a nocturnal nightjar found from Mexico through Central America and much of South America. It is named for its distinctive repeated calls, often heard after dusk or before dawn. The species spends the day resting motionless on leaf litter or other shaded ground, where its mottled plumage provides excellent camouflage. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread resident and is often encountered in warm lowland habitats, especially along forest edges, roads, clearings, and other partly open areas.
value.classification: The Common Pauraque belongs to the nightjar family Caprimulgidae, a group of insect-eating birds adapted to evening and nighttime activity. Its scientific name is Nyctidromus albicollis.
value.identification: This medium-sized nightjar has cryptic plumage in mottled brown, gray, buff, and rufous tones. It has a broad, rounded wing, a long rounded tail, a short bill with a wide gape, and large dark eyes. A pale throat patch is visible, especially when the bird calls, and white markings may show on the outer tail feathers in flight. It is usually detected by its repeated, distinctive nocturnal whistle rather than by sight.
value.rangeHabitat: The Common Pauraque ranges from Mexico through Central America to much of South America, including Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica it is a common to abundant resident across much of the country, mainly in the lowlands and locally up to about 1,700 meters. It uses dry and moist forest, woodland, scrub, forest edges, plantations, pastures with scattered trees, clearings, and unpaved roads. It often favors open ground near cover where it can forage and rest.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident and does not undertake a regular long-distance migration. Common Pauraques occur year-round in Costa Rica, although local movements and seasonal changes in detectability or abundance may occur.
value.breeding: The Common Pauraque lays its eggs directly on leaf litter or bare ground, without constructing a conventional nest. A clutch normally contains two eggs, which are buff or salmon-buff and marked with reddish-brown, cinnamon, gray, and lavender tones. The female relies on camouflage, while adults may distract predators by moving away from the eggs or young. Breeding timing varies across the broad range and is influenced by local rainfall and seasonal conditions; the species breeds in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of flying insects, including moths, beetles, bugs, and other small arthropods. It commonly waits on the ground, a low perch, or a roadside and then makes short, rapid flights to capture prey in the air. Feeding is concentrated around dusk, during the night, and before dawn. Artificial lights may attract insects and can sometimes bring the species close to buildings or roads.
value.behavior: The Common Pauraque is primarily crepuscular and nocturnal. During daylight it rests quietly on the ground or on a low branch, remaining difficult to see because of its camouflage. At dusk it becomes active, flying low over roads, clearings, and woodland edges. Its repeated, musical call is one of the easiest ways to locate it. Adults may flutter, call, or feign injury near a nest or young to draw attention away from them.
